e.t: This word is a proper name referring to a person named Abimeel, also rendered Avimil. It functions as an individual’s name rather than as a description, action, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Genesis 10:28. The name itself does not provide enough information here to explain the person’s character, role, or significance; those details would require the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “message”: information or news communicated from one person or place to another. It is a noun, so it names the message itself rather than the person delivering it or the act of delivering it. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 13 times, chiefly in Old Testament passages, and can refer generally to communicated news. The surrounding verse determines whether the message is joyful, troubling, urgent, or informative; the word itself identifies the communication being conveyed.

Adid, also rendered Athith, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Nehemiah 7:37. The available form preserves the name itself, while the two renderings reflect ways of representing that name in English. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person or group being identified there.

This Greek LXX noun means “its porch,” referring to a porch or entrance structure belonging to something else. It appears 16 times in the Greek Old Testament, all in Ezekiel 40, where the word is used repeatedly in descriptions of the temple’s measured entrances and surrounding architectural features. The pronoun-like element in the gloss points to a porch connected with a particular gate or structure, rather than a standalone place. Its precise reference is determined by the surrounding architectural description.

This Greek LXX verb means “hurl a javelin,” describing the act of throwing a spear-like weapon through the air. It names a specific physical action rather than a general movement or attack. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX, all within three verses of 1 Samuel 20. Its precise force in any one sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the throwing or launching of a javelin.

Halikarnassos, also called Alikarnassos, is a proper name for a place. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it appears once, in 1 Maccabees 15:23. The word itself identifies the location rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its particular role in that passage cannot be explained further; its basic meaning is the place name Halikarnassos.

This noun means “drawing back” or “retreat”—a movement away from a place, position, or situation. It describes withdrawal rather than advance, and its basic sense is physical or directional unless the surrounding passage gives it a more specific force. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 19:7. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s precise role in that passage cannot be stated beyond this central meaning.

This adverb describes acting manfully or courageously—with firmness, bravery, and resolve. It tells how someone carries out an action rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 6:27. Its central idea is courageous conduct: facing a demanding situation with strength instead of shrinking back. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the specific action it describes there.

Anna is a personal name, referring to a woman named Anna rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears eight times across seven verses, all in 1 Samuel 1. The name is used consistently as “Anna,” identifying the same woman throughout these occurrences. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning and function are simply a woman’s personal name.

This Greek LXX verb means “dig up”: to excavate or bring something out of the ground. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament represented here, both times in Job, at Job 3:21 and Job 39:21. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary sense remains the physical act of digging into the earth and uncovering what is beneath it.

This Greek LXX verb means “kindle a light in turn.” It describes the action of causing light to be kindled as part of a reciprocal or successive action. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 1:32. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is the turning on or kindling of light in response or succession.

This LXX word means “before” or “contrary,” describing something positioned in front of, opposite to, or facing another. It can function as an adverb or preposition, helping show location or direction in a sentence. The word occurs 86 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, with “before” appearing as a common English rendering. Its exact sense in a particular verse depends on what person, place, or thing it stands in relation to.

This verb means to tithe: to give or set apart a tenth. It describes the act of assigning one part in ten, especially in the Old Testament passages concerning produce, possessions, or resources. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, all in six verses. Its sense is consistent wherever it appears, while the surrounding passage identifies what is being tithed and for whom it is designated.

This Greek verb means to pluck grapes or other fruit. It describes the act of gathering fruit directly from a plant, rather than a general idea of harvesting or collecting food. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Amos 6:1. Because the word appears only there and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the larger passage. Its basic meaning remains the physical action of plucking ripe fruit.

This adjective describes someone who is undaunted—remaining firm rather than being overcome by fear, pressure, or difficulty. It presents a person as courageous and steady in the face of what might discourage or frighten others. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, at Jeremiah 27:2. That reference locates its use, while the surrounding verse is needed to show precisely whom or what it describes there.

This adjective means “made by a baker.” It describes something prepared or produced by a person whose work is baking, rather than naming the baker himself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 16:3. The exact thing it describes must be understood from the surrounding verse, but its basic sense points to an item associated with a baker’s work. This is a specific descriptive word, not a broad term for all food or every kind of preparation.

Astin is a personal name, referring to the individual identified by that name in the Greek Old Testament text of Esther. It is not a word describing an action, quality, or object; it functions as a proper name. Astin occurs seven times in the LXX, all within Esther, from Esther 1:9 through Esther 2:4. Its precise role in any one verse depends on the surrounding text.

This adjective means “without end,” describing something that has no ending or completion. It expresses an unending quality rather than naming a person, place, or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in the book of Wisdom. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise reference in each passage depends on the sentence where it appears; the central idea remains that the thing described continues without an end.

This verb means “take away”: to remove something, carry it off, or cause it to be taken from its place. It describes an action of removal rather than merely seeing, changing, or possessing something. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 155 times, mostly in the Old Testament portion of the LXX, and is also found in deuterocanonical writings. Its exact object and force depend on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains taking something away or removing it.

This adjective means “uncorrupt,” describing something that has not been spoiled, damaged, or defiled. It points to a condition of soundness and freedom from corruption rather than describing an action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Esther 2:2. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains something uncorrupt or untouched by corruption.

Achichōd, also rendered Akhikhoth, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a particular person named in 1 Chronicles 8:7. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, so its ordinary lexical significance is limited to identifying that individual; the surrounding verse is needed to explain the person’s specific place in the genealogy.

This word means “helper”: a person or one who provides assistance and support. As a noun in the Greek Old Testament, it identifies someone who comes alongside another to give needed aid. It occurs 49 times in this LXX corpus, so it is used broadly for human assistance and for those regarded as dependable support. Its basic sense remains focused on helping rather than describing a particular kind of task or relationship.

Gethchober is a proper name, also rendered Yethkhover. It identifies a specific named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. This Greek LXX word occurs once, in 2 Kings 14:25. Because the available information does not provide the verse text or further explanation of the named entity, its precise referent must be understood from that passage. The word itself functions as a name, while the two supplied renderings represent alternate ways of presenting it in English.

Geseel, also rendered Yesil, is a proper name referring to a person named in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at 1 Chronicles 4:16. Because it is a personal name rather than a common noun or action word, its meaning is primarily identification: it distinguishes this individual from others in the genealogical record. The name itself does not express a general quality, action, or spiritual concept.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Gēra” or “Yira.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical corpus, it occurs 14 times, beginning in Genesis and continuing through Sirach. The available passages preserve it as a personal designation, so its normal meaning is the name itself: Gera, also represented as Yira. The surrounding verse is needed to identify which individual bears the name in a particular occurrence.

This adjective means “naked,” describing a person who has no clothing or covering. It can identify someone as physically unclothed, whether plainly visible or lacking the protection normally provided by garments. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 33 times, with the same central sense. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the ordinary idea remains being without clothing or covering.

Dasem, also rendered Thasem, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person or place by name rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Genesis 10:12. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain its particular referent or significance more precisely.

This Greek LXX verb means “shake down”: to shake someone or something forcefully, often with the sense of making something fall or loosening what is held. It is a verb describing an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 7:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This noun means “justifying” or “justification”: it names the act or condition of being declared or shown right. It refers to justification as a matter being expressed, discussed, or recognized, rather than functioning as a command or action-word itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice, in Leviticus and Sirach, so its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This noun describes cunning or treachery: a deceptive, faithless approach intended to mislead or harm. It points to crafty behavior rather than open and honest dealing. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs 53 times, showing that this idea appears across many passages and settings. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central meaning remains deceitful cunning or treacherous conduct.

“Bear with pain; bear ill” is a verb describing someone enduring distress or suffering hardship. It points to the experience of finding something painful or difficult to endure, rather than simply naming pain itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains enduring what causes suffering.

Easakem is a proper name—a personal or place name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 9:4. The available meaning is simply the name “Easakem”; Scripture does not provide an additional definition or explanation of the name itself. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context, which are handled separately from the word’s basic lexical identity.

This Greek verb means “persevere”: to continue faithfully and steadily instead of giving up. It describes persistent endurance, especially when a person remains committed through difficulty or delay. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 14:9. The surrounding sentence determines what the perseverance involves.

gl: make like to; represent by a likeness
d: make like to; represent by a likeness

e.t: To make something like another thing, or to represent it by a likeness, is the basic meaning of this LXX verb. It describes shaping or presenting something so that it resembles something else. The word occurs four times in this LXX corpus, in Jeremiah and Wisdom, so its meaning is clear but its use is relatively uncommon. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse.

gl: on each side; on either hand
d: on each side; on either hand

e.t: This Greek LXX adverb means “on each side” or “on either hand.” It points to something situated, occurring, or extending on both sides, or to two sides considered separately. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX material, both in 4 Maccabees. Because verse text is not provided here, its precise force in either occurrence depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central directional meaning remains the same.

This Greek LXX verb means “excite to war” or “make hostile.” It describes causing people or groups to become enemies or stirring them toward armed conflict. The word is used eleven times in the Greek Old Testament and related writings, including passages about nations preparing for conflict and hostility being directed against others. Its focus is active provocation: someone or something produces a warlike or hostile response rather than merely experiencing conflict. The exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Escape means getting away from danger, trouble, or confinement. As a noun, it names the act or possibility of escaping rather than the person who escapes. This Greek Old Testament word occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Job 15:30, and its recorded rendering is “escape.” Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains a way out or release from what threatens or holds someone.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Eliadae” or “Eliathae.” It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament (LXX), rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs once in this LXX corpus, at 1 Kings 11:14. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be explained further, but its basic function is clear: it is a personal name.

This Greek LXX verb means “roll up in,” describing the action of wrapping or enclosing something within another thing. It expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Samuel 21:10. Its basic sense is specific and concrete: something is rolled or wrapped inside something else. The surrounding verse is needed to explain exactly what is being enclosed and how the action functions there.

This Greek LXX verb means “settle in.” It describes the act of taking up residence or becoming established in a place, rather than merely passing through it. Its basic sense is practical and straightforward: someone or something comes to dwell in a particular location. The word occurs once in the LXX corpus, in Sirach 11:34. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the specific situation, but the word itself expresses settling in or establishing a dwelling.

This verb means “follow”—to go after someone or something, or to continue in the same direction or course. It can describe physical following, but its ordinary sense also fits following a person’s way, conduct, or instruction. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times: five times in Old Testament books and once in Sirach. Its central idea remains straightforward: directing oneself after another rather than going independently.

This Greek LXX verb means “creep out of,” describing the act of slowly or quietly coming out from something. It functions as an action word, focusing on movement from within or away from an enclosing place. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 104:30. The precise force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but the word itself presents a gradual emergence rather than a sudden departure.

This verb means “gather together; collect.” It describes bringing people or things together rather than leaving them scattered. As a verb, it expresses an action of assembling or collecting. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, so its basic meaning is clear even though its precise force in any particular passage depends on what is being gathered and the surrounding context.

This adjective means “painful,” describing something that causes or involves pain. It is a descriptive word rather than the name of an action or person, so its precise force depends on the noun or situation it modifies. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 14:10. The word’s central sense remains straightforward: it identifies something as painful or distressing in nature.

This word is an adjective that describes a quality or condition. Its basic sense is “remaining time”. It points to time that is still left or available, rather than time already completed. As an adjective, it describes something in relation to that remaining period. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 18 times, showing regular use for what continues after an earlier portion has passed.

“Limp on” means to move forward with an uneven or impaired step. It is a verb describing the act of continuing to walk while limping, rather than moving normally. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Genesis 32:32. Its basic meaning identifies a physical manner of movement; the surrounding verse is needed to explain the specific situation in which it occurs. The supplied lexical definition directly supports this sense.

This word is the proper name “Eselias.” It functions as a name rather than a word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in 2 Kings 22:3. Because it is a personal name with no additional lexical definition given, its main meaning is simply the identification of someone called Eselias; the surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s role.

This adjective describes someone who has reached extreme old age. It points to the final or most advanced stage of a person’s years, rather than simply indicating that someone is older. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Sirach 42:8. The word’s basic emphasis is the exceptional fullness or extremity of age. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This adjective means “obedient,” describing a person who complies with what is commanded or expected. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs twice, once in Proverbs and once in the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its central idea is a posture of obedience; the surrounding verse is needed to identify who is described and what command or expectation is involved. It is not itself a title or name, but a describing word.

This noun refers to setting something straight or bringing it into proper order; it can therefore be understood as correction. Its central idea is a needed adjustment rather than a vague improvement: something is put right. In the Greek Old Testament translation tradition, it appears twice, both in 3 Maccabees. The word’s exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, which is not included here, but its basic meaning remains the act or result of correction.

This noun means “vigour,” referring to strength, energy, or robust force. It describes a quality of energetic power rather than an action or person by itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Ecclesiastes 7:7. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is vigorous strength.

This noun refers to someone equal in age or regarded as a fellow. It identifies a person in relation to another person, emphasizing shared age or companionship rather than a personal name or title. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 11:14. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is someone of the same age or a companion.

Ēsarei, also given as Isari, is a personal name rather than a general description or action. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Chronicles 2:54. Because the available wording identifies the name but does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, its specific family connection and role there cannot be explained from the name alone.

This word means “incense altar,” referring to an altar or altar-like place used in connection with burning incense. It is a noun in the Greek Old Testament and related writings, so it names a sacred object rather than an action or quality. The word occurs three times in this Greek corpus, in passages from 2 Chronicles, Ezekiel, and 4 Maccabees. Its exact significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene.

Iaphalet, also rendered Iafalit, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within the genealogical records of 1 Chronicles 7:32–33. The name appears once in verse 32 and twice in verse 33. Its precise significance as a name is not explained by the available biblical wording, so it is best understood simply as the name of a person in that genealogy.

Ieblaam, also written Ievlaam, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a place rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The name occurs three times in the Septuagint, in Judges, 2 Kings, and 1 Chronicles. Its exact significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and narrative, but the word itself functions as a geographical name. The two forms are simply variant renderings of the same place-name in this corpus.

Iemain, also rendered “Iemen,” is a proper name used to identify a named entity in the Greek Old Testament. Its exact referent cannot be described further from the available lexical information alone. This word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Joshua 15:53. As a name, it functions differently from an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object; its meaning is primarily its identifying designation in that passage.

Ioida, also rendered Iitha, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, object, or general idea. This name occurs once in the Greek text, in Nehemiah 3:6. The reference confirms where the name appears, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain that person’s specific role or connection in the passage. As a proper name, its meaning is chiefly its identification of a particular person.

gl: equally animated; with the same soul
d: equally animated; with the same soul

e.t: This adjective describes people who are “equally animated; with the same soul.” It points to a close likeness in inward life, feeling, or disposition rather than merely outward agreement. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at Psalm 54:14. Because the verse text is not included here, its precise role in that sentence must be understood from the surrounding context. Its basic sense is shared inward life and sympathy.

Issachar is a proper name, referring to the biblical figure and the people identified by his name. Its stated meaning is “Issachar,” with “Issakhar” as an alternate rendering. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears 40 times across 39 verses, from Genesis through Ezekiel. It is especially frequent in Numbers and 1 Chronicles, where the name identifies Issachar within Israel’s recorded family and tribal history.

This verb means to empty out—to remove what is inside a container or space. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, appearing in Genesis and 2 Samuel. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the act of making something empty by pouring, removing, or taking its contents away.

This Greek Old Testament word means “set in order” or “arrange.” It is a verb describing the act of putting things into a proper, orderly arrangement rather than leaving them disorganized. The word appears three times in the Greek Septuagint corpus, in Exodus, Isaiah, and 1 Maccabees. Its basic sense can apply wherever people or objects are organized into a fitting order; the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being arranged.

This verb means to take up one’s quarters or encamp—to settle in a place as a dwelling or camp. It describes establishing residence, whether temporarily like a camp or more securely as a dwelling. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, all in Old Testament verses, and its use can refer to people taking their place or to dwelling in a location. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on settling, camping, or taking up a particular place.

This adjective means “of clay” or “ceramic,” describing something made from clay. It identifies a material rather than an action, person, or abstract quality. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Daniel 2:41. Its basic sense points to an object formed from clay or pottery material. The surrounding verse is needed to explain exactly what the adjective describes there.

This Greek Old Testament noun means a pole, specifically a punting-pole. It refers to a long, sturdy implement used for pushing or supporting something, rather than expressing an action or quality. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in 1 Samuel 17:7 and once in Ezekiel 39:9. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains a physical pole or staff-like object.

This verb means “create” or “set up,” describing the act of bringing something into existence or establishing it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it is used for God’s creative work and for the establishment or arrangement of things. It occurs 61 times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages in Genesis, Psalms, Isaiah, and later biblical books. Its precise force in any sentence depends on what is being created or established there.

gl: drive away cattle as booty; make booty
d: drive away cattle as booty; make booty

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means to drive away cattle as booty—to seize livestock and carry it off as spoils. It describes an act of taking animals during plunder or conflict, rather than simply moving or tending them. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 2:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning centers on capturing cattle and treating them as recovered or seized booty.

This Greek LXX adjective means “thin.” It describes something having little thickness or a slender appearance, rather than being broad or substantial. The word occurs 28 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings, with uses beginning in Genesis and continuing through Wisdom. Its exact force depends on the thing being described, but its central idea remains physical thinness or leanness. It is distinct here as a Greek LXX word, not a Greek New Testament entity.

This Greek LXX verb means “cook” or, more specifically, “cook meat.” It describes the action of preparing food by cooking it. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented by the LXX, in Lamentations 2:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is the practical act of cooking, especially preparing meat as food.

This noun means an “oracle”—a declared message or answer sought from a divine source. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Proverbs 16:10 and Ezekiel 21:27. Those references show that the word belongs to language about pronouncement, but the precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage. It is a rare term in this corpus, yet its central idea remains clear: an oracle is a message presented as coming from divine authority.

Maselmoth is a proper name, referring to a person or named figure identified by that name. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 9:12. The available wording preserves the name as “Maselmoth,” rather than translating it into an ordinary descriptive term. Its precise identity and role must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage, since the name alone does not state what the person did or why the name is mentioned.

This adjective describes someone or something as fit for battle—warlike and prepared for fighting. It can characterize people or forces according to their readiness and suitability for warfare. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, especially in Joshua, with additional occurrences in 2 Kings and Proverbs. Its basic sense is martial capability rather than a particular battle or action; the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being described.

This Greek LXX verb means “get drunk,” describing becoming intoxicated through drinking. It refers to a person entering or being in a state of drunkenness, rather than naming a drink itself. The word occurs 46 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, so it is used across a range of passages rather than being limited to one setting. Its first listed occurrence is Genesis 9:21, and its final listed occurrence is Song of Songs 5:1; the precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This verb means being “concerned with” something. It describes directing one’s attention or thought toward a matter, rather than merely mentioning it. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 33 times, so it is a recurring word for mental or practical involvement. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains active concern with a subject or matter.

This Greek LXX verb means “educate differently,” describing a change in the way someone is taught or instructed. It presents education as being redirected or conducted by another approach rather than simply repeated in the same manner. The word occurs once in the Greek text of 4 Maccabees, at 4 Maccabees 2:7. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense concerns altering or redirecting instruction.

This noun means “thigh,” the upper part of the leg between the hip and knee. It refers to a specific part of the human body and is used in the Greek Old Testament to identify that bodily area in ordinary descriptions and actions. The word occurs 33 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, with appearances across books including Genesis, Judges, Ezekiel, and Numbers. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the body part called the thigh.

This noun refers to the nostrils—the openings of the nose. It names a specific part of the body rather than an action, feeling, or broader idea. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Zechariah 4:12. The word’s basic meaning remains straightforward: it identifies the nose openings through which a person breathes. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the actual wording there.

Nabousaris; Navusaris is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament tradition. It identifies a particular named referent rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Jeremiah 46:3. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not describe the person or thing identified, so its precise referent must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

Odomēra, also rendered Othomira, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular named figure or entity in the Greek LXX corpus. This form occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 9:66. Without the verse text, the name alone does not establish whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity; its precise identification belongs to the surrounding passage.

“Compassionate” describes someone who responds with deep concern toward those who suffer or need help. This word can function as an adjective describing a compassionate person, or as a noun referring to someone characterized by compassion. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 21 times, showing a repeated description of compassionate character rather than a single isolated use. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Ommaios” or “Ommeos.” It identifies a named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Genesis 14:5. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide an additional ordinary definition or explanation of its origin. Its precise significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage.

This adjective means “upright” or “normal.” It can describe something standing or directed in a straight, proper way, and it can also describe what is ordinary or fitting rather than distorted or unusual. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 26 times, chiefly in Proverbs, where its basic idea suits language about a straight path, a proper direction, or what is sound and right. The precise force in any verse depends on the noun or action it describes.

Oudia is a proper name, also rendered “Uthia.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 28:12. Because the available wording gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its specific role in that passage cannot be described further here.
